context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Grounding Techniques

title: 2. Understanding Your Responses
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Understanding Different Types of Trauma
text: Your symptoms make sense as adaptations to what you experienced: - Hypervigilance kept you alert to danger - Avoidance protected you from overwhelming feelings - Dissociation helped you survive the unsurvivable

title: 3. Regulating the Nervous System
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Understanding Different Types of Trauma

title: 4. Processing Traumatic Memory
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Understanding Different Types of Trauma
text: When ready, trauma can be processed through: - Telling the story in safe contexts - Trauma-focused therapies (EMDR, CPT, PE, Somatic Experiencing) - Gradual exposure to avoided triggers - Making meaning of what happened

title: 5. Rebuilding Connection
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Understanding Different Types of Trauma
text: Trauma often damages our capacity for connection: - Learning to trust again (starting small) - Developing healthy relationships - Connecting with community - Healing relational trauma in relationships

title: 6. Reclaiming Identity
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Understanding Different Types of Trauma
text: Moving from "trauma survivor" to a more expansive identity: - Discovering who you are beyond trauma - Building a life aligned with your values - Finding meaning and purpose - Post-traumatic growth is possible ---

title: Common Misconceptions
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance

title: "I should always be in my window"
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance
text: No. Life includes stress, challenge, and difficult emotions. Sometimes leaving your window is appropriate—you just want to be able to return.

title: "The goal is to never feel anxious or sad"
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance
text: No. The goal is to feel the full range of human emotions without being overwhelmed by them or shutting down from them. Emotions are information.

title: "If I'm not in my window, I'm failing"
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance
text: No. Noticing you're outside your window IS success. That awareness is the first step to change.

title: "I should be able to widen my window faster"
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance
text: Recovery takes time. Your nervous system learned these patterns over years, often decades. Be patient with the process.

title: "Widening my window means becoming less sensitive"
context: Chapter 1 · Understanding Trauma & Basic Recovery · Window of Tolerance
text: No. It often means feeling MORE—you can finally feel your emotions instead of being overwhelmed by them or numb to them.

title: The Urge Surfing Technique
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing

title: Step 1: Notice the Urge
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: When a craving arises, pause and acknowledge it: - "I'm noticing an urge to use" - "There's a craving present right now" - "My mind is telling me I need [substance/behavior]" Simply naming the experience creates distance between you and the urge.

context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Urges always have physical components. Scan your body and notice: - Where do you feel the urge? (chest, stomach, throat, etc.) - What does it feel like? (tightness, heat, pressure, restlessness) - How intense is it on a scale of 1-10? Common physical locations

title: Step 3: Focus on Your Breath
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Bring attention to your breathing without trying to change it: - Notice the natural rhythm of inhale and exhale - Feel the breath moving in and out of your body - Let breathing be an anchor as you observe the urge

title: Step 4: Surf the Wave
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Now, observe the urge as if you're watching a wave: - Notice as it rises in intensity - Watch it reach its peak - Observe as it begins to subside - Continue watching until it passes Key mindset shifts: - "I am not the urge—I am the observer of the urge" - "Thi

title: Step 5: Repeat as Needed
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Urges may come in multiple waves. Each time: - Return to observing - Notice any changes in location or intensity - Continue surfing until the wave passes ---

title: Combining Urge Surfing with Other Techniques
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing

title: HALT Check First
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Before surfing, quickly assess: - Hungry? Eat something first - Angry? Acknowledge the emotion - Lonely? Reach out to someone - Tired? Rest if possible Addressing these basic needs can reduce urge intensity before you begin surfing.

title: Grounding Before Surfing
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: If the urge feels overwhelming, ground yourself first: - 5-4-3-2-1 technique (5 things you see, 4 you hear, etc.) - Cold water on wrists or face - Feel your feet on the ground Then transition to urge surfing.

title: After the Wave Passes
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Once the urge subsides: - Acknowledge your success: "I rode that out" - Notice how you feel now - Consider what triggered the urge - Engage in a recovery-supportive activity ---

title: Building Your Urge Surfing Practice

title: Daily Practice (Even Without Urges)
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing

title: Keep a Craving Log
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: Track your urges to learn patterns: Over time, you'll notice: - Common triggers - Typical duration - What helps and what doesn't - Progress in your ability to surf ---

title: Common Challenges and Solutions
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing

title: "The urge feels too strong"
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: - Start with grounding techniques first - Focus on just one breath at a time - Remind yourself: "This will pass" - Call your sponsor or support person

title: "I can't focus on breathing"
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: - Try opening your eyes and focusing on an object - Use a physical anchor (holding something textured) - Count your breaths to maintain focus

title: "Multiple waves keep coming"
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: - This is normal, especially early in recovery - Each wave you surf without using weakens the next - Persistence pays off—cravings diminish over time

title: "I'm too anxious to sit still"
context: Chapter 3 · Addiction Recovery · Urge Surfing
text: - Try walking urge surfing—observe while moving slowly - Focus on the physical sensations of walking - Return to breath when possible ---

title: Common Cognitive Distortions
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Our thoughts aren't always accurate reflections of reality. Trauma, stress, anxiety, and depression can create distorted thinking patterns that fuel negative cycles.

title: All-or-Nothing Thinking
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "If I'm not perfect, I'm a complete failure." Reality: Most things exist on a spectrum. There's vast territory between perfect and failure.

title: Catastrophizing
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "This headache means something terrible. Everything is going to fall apart." Reality: Jumping to worst-case scenarios creates unnecessary suffering. Most fears don't materialize.

title: Mind Reading
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "They think I'm pathetic. I can tell by how they looked at me." Reality: You can't actually know what others think without asking. Assumptions are often wrong.

title: Emotional Reasoning
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "I feel like a failure, so I must be one." Reality: Feelings are real, but they don't define truth. You can feel something intensely and it can still be inaccurate.

title: Should Statements
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "I should be over this by now. I shouldn't feel this way." Reality: "Shoulds" create shame and pressure. Working with reality is more effective than demanding it be different.

title: Personalization
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "My friend is quiet today. I must have done something to upset them." Reality: Other people's moods and behaviors are usually about their own experiences, not about you.

title: Overgeneralization
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · The CBT Triangle
text: Pattern: "I messed up this presentation. I always fail at everything important." Reality: One event doesn't define a pattern. "Always" and "never" are rarely accurate. ---

title: How to Challenge Cognitive Distortions
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions

title: Step 1: Notice and Name
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: You can't change what you don't see. Start building awareness: - Keep a thought log - Notice when you feel a sudden mood shift - Pay attention to thoughts that start with "always," "never," "should," or "I'm" - Identify which distortions you use most often

title: Step 2: Examine the Evidence
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: Ask yourself: - What evidence supports this thought? - What evidence contradicts it? - Am I looking at the full picture or filtering? - Would a fair judge agree with my interpretation? - What would I tell a friend who had this thought?

title: Step 3: Generate Alternatives
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: - What are other possible explanations? - What's the most realistic interpretation? - What's a more balanced way to view this? - What would be a compassionate perspective?

title: Step 4: Test It Out
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: - What would happen if I acted as if the alternative thought were true? - Can I run an experiment to gather more information? - What have similar situations taught me in the past?

title: Step 5: Create a Balanced Thought
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions

title: Common Pitfalls
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions

title: Pitfall 1: Using Challenging Distortions as Self-Attack
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: "I shouldn't think this way. What's wrong with me?" is just another distortion. Approach your thoughts with curiosity, not judgment.

title: Pitfall 2: Expecting Immediate Belief
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: You don't have to fully believe the balanced thought at first. Your emotional brain needs time to catch up. Keep practicing.

title: Pitfall 3: Forgetting Context
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: When you're triggered, exhausted, hungry, or in pain, cognitive work is harder. Sometimes you need to regulate your body first, then challenge thoughts later.

title: Pitfall 4: Trying to Eliminate All Negative Thoughts
context: Chapter 8 · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) · Cognitive Distortions
text: The goal isn't to only think positive thoughts. Negative thoughts are normal. The goal is to not let distorted thoughts run your life unchecked. ---

title: Wise Mind

text: Wise Mind is one of the most important concepts in DBT. It represents the integration of emotion and reason—the inner wisdom that combines heart and head.

title: Reasonable Mind

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT)
text: Interpersonal effectiveness skills help you navigate relationships, get your needs met, maintain self-respect, and build healthy connections with others.

title: Goals of Interpersonal Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: In any interpersonal interaction, you may have three goals:

title: 1. Objectives Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Getting what you want or need from the interaction. - Achieving a tangible outcome - Having your request granted - Saying no to an unwanted request

title: 2. Relationship Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Maintaining or improving the relationship. - Keeping the relationship positive - The other person still liking/respecting you - Not damaging the connection

title: 3. Self-Respect Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Maintaining your self-respect. - Acting in line with your values - Feeling good about yourself afterward - Not compromising your integrity The Challenge: Sometimes these goals conflict. You might get what you want but damage the relationship. Or you might keep

title: DEAR MAN: Getting What You Want
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: DEAR MAN is for objectives effectiveness—getting your needs met or saying no.

title: D - Describe
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Describe the situation factually. - Stick to objective facts - No judgments or interpretations - What happened? What did you observe? Example: - NOT: "You always ignore me" - YES: "I've texted you three times this week and haven't gotten a response"

title: E - Express
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Express your feelings and opinions. - Use "I" statements - Share how you feel - Don't expect others to read your mind Example: - "I feel worried when I don't hear back" - "I'm frustrated because I need your input on this"

title: A - Assert
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Assert what you want or don't want. - Ask clearly for what you need - Say no clearly if needed - Don't assume they know - Be specific Example: - "I would like you to respond within 24 hours, even just to say you'll get back to me later" - "I'm not able to take

title: R - Reinforce
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Reinforce (reward) the person for responding. - Explain benefits of giving you what you want - Explain consequences of not - Make it worth their while Example: - "If you can let me know you got my message, I won't worry and won't need to follow up" - "I'd real

title: M - Stay Mindful
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Stay mindful of your goals. - Don't get distracted - Return to your point if they change the subject - Broken record: calmly repeat your request Technique - Broken Record: Calmly repeat your request or no, regardless of what the other person says: - "I underst

title: A - Appear Confident
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Appear confident in your manner. - Maintain eye contact - Speak clearly, not too quietly - Stand/sit upright - Act as if you deserve what you're asking for Even if you don't feel confident, acting confident increases effectiveness.

title: N - Negotiate
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Be willing to negotiate. - Be open to alternatives - Ask for their ideas - Turn the tables: "What do you suggest?" - Reduce your request or offer something Example: - "If you can't do all of it, could you do this part?" - "What would work for you?" ---

title: GIVE: Relationship Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: GIVE helps maintain and improve relationships.

title: G - Be Gentle
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Be gentle in your approach. - No attacks or threats - No judgments or name-calling - No sarcasm or sneering - Respect the other person Even when asserting yourself, you can be gentle.

title: I - Act Interested
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Act interested in the other person. - Listen actively - Face them, make eye contact - Don't interrupt - Ask questions - Validate their perspective People are more responsive when they feel heard.

title: V - Validate
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Validate their feelings, thoughts, and perspective. - Acknowledge their experience - Show you understand where they're coming from - Don't dismiss or minimize - You can validate without agreeing Examples: - "I can see why you'd feel that way" - "That makes sen

title: E - Use an Easy Manner
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Use an easy, non-threatening manner. - Lighten up if appropriate - Use humor if it fits - Smile when appropriate - Be relaxed - Ease along rather than forcing A lighter touch often works better than intensity. ---

title: FAST: Self-Respect Effectiveness
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: FAST helps you maintain self-respect in interactions.

title: F - Be Fair
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Be fair to yourself and the other person. - Consider both sides - Don't be a doormat - Don't be a bully either - Balance your needs with theirs

title: A - No Apologies (Unnecessary)
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Don't over-apologize. - Don't apologize for having needs - Don't apologize for making a request - Don't apologize for saying no - Apologize only when you've done something wrong Over-apologizing undermines your self-respect and your message.

title: S - Stick to Values
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Stick to your values. - Don't compromise your integrity - Don't agree to things that violate your values - Don't sacrifice self-respect for approval - Stay true to what matters to you

title: T - Be Truthful
context: Chapter 9 · Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) · Interpersonal Effectiveness
text: Be honest. - Don't lie or manipulate - Don't exaggerate - Don't act helpless when you're not - Speak your truth Lying undermines self-respect and relationships. ---

context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · EMDR Therapy

title: Overview
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · EMDR Therapy

title: How It Works
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · EMDR Therapy
text: EMDR uses bilateral stimulation (typically eye movements, but also taps or auditory tones) while the client briefly focuses on a traumatic memory. This appears to help the brain process "stuck" memories and integrate them in a healthier way. The theory behind

title: The Eight Phases of EMDR
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · EMDR Therapy

title: TMS Therapy
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies
text: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive brain stimulation technique that uses magnetic fields to stimulate nerve cells in the brain. It represents a different approach to mental health treatment—working directly on brain circuitry.

title: What is TMS?
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · TMS Therapy

title: Overview
context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · TMS Therapy

context: Chapter 11 · Alternative Therapies · TMS Therapy

title: Morning Prayers

title: Traditional Morning Prayer
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Lord, help me to remember today that nothing is going to happen that you and I together can't handle. Grant me the courage to meet whatever comes with calm assurance, knowing you are by my side. Amen.

title: Non-Theistic Morning Intention
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Today I set the intention to stay present, to be kind to myself and others, to do the next right thing, and to ask for help when I need it. I choose recovery today. I am open to growth and learning. May I be a source of light in the world.

title: Prayers for Difficult Moments
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations

title: When Craving
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Higher Power, I am struggling right now. Help me remember why I chose recovery. Give me the strength to get through this moment. Help me reach out for support. May this craving pass, as all things pass. I choose recovery, one moment at a time.

title: When Tempted
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Grant me the wisdom to see this situation clearly. Help me remember the pain my addiction has caused. Give me the strength to walk away. Remind me of who I want to become. Guide my feet in the direction of my recovery.

title: In Gratitude
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Thank you for another day clean and sober. Thank you for the progress I've made. Thank you for the people who support me. Thank you for the gift of awareness. Thank you for the chance to begin again. May I never take my recovery for granted.

title: For Those Still Suffering
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: May all who struggle with addiction find their way to recovery. May those who suffer find relief. May those who are lost find their path. May those who have given up find hope again. May compassion extend to all beings everywhere. ---

title: Evening Prayers
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations

title: Traditional Evening Prayer
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: Lord, as I end this day, I thank you for your presence with me. Forgive me for the times I fell short. Help me to let go of the day's troubles and rest peacefully. Watch over me and those I love through the night. Amen.

title: Evening Reflection (Non-Theistic)
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: As this day ends, I reflect on my actions with honesty and without harsh judgment. Where I acted in line with my values, I feel gratitude. Where I fell short, I commit to learning and doing better. I release this day and open to rest.

title: Metta (Loving-Kindness) Practice
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: May I be happy. May I be healthy. May I be safe. May I live with ease. May all beings be happy. May all beings be healthy. May all beings be safe. May all beings live with ease. ---

title: Meditation Practices
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations

title: Simple Breath Awareness
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: 1. Sit comfortably with a straight back 2. Close your eyes or soften your gaze 3. Bring attention to your breath 4. Notice the in-breath, the out-breath 5. When mind wanders, gently return to breath 6. Practice for 5-20 minutes

title: Body Scan for Recovery
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: 1. Lie down or sit comfortably 2. Start at the top of your head 3. Slowly move attention down through your body 4. Notice sensations without trying to change them 5. Include areas of tension or discomfort 6. End with awareness of the whole body

title: Gratitude Meditation
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: 1. Sit comfortably and close your eyes 2. Bring to mind something you're grateful for 3. Feel the gratitude in your body 4. Expand to another thing, then another 5. Include small things and large things 6. Rest in the feeling of gratitude

title: Walking Meditation
context: Chapter 12 · Spirituality in Recovery · Recovery Prayers & Meditations
text: 1. Find a path of 20-30 feet 2. Stand at one end, feeling your feet 3. Walk very slowly and deliberately 4. Notice each component: lifting, moving, placing 5. At the end, pause and turn 6. Walk back with the same attention 7. Continue for 10-20 minutes ---
